html:
Malaya is the old name for the Malay Peninsula south of Siam, together here with the north coast of Borneo. The map shows it from 1650 to 1914, when it was a set of Malay sultanates that came step by step under British control.

After Portugal took Malacca in 1511, the heirs of its royal house founded Johor. In 1641 the Dutch East India Company took Malacca from the Portuguese with Johor's help. Other sultanates held the river valleys: Kedah, Perak with its tin, Pahang, Terengganu and Kelantan. The northern ones sent tribute to Siam. In the 1700s Bugis warriors from Sulawesi became powerful in Johor.

Britain came for trade and a route to China:

  • Francis Light founded George Town on Penang in 1786.
  • Stamford Raffles founded modern Singapore in 1819.
  • The Anglo Dutch Treaty of 1824 split the Malay world along the Strait of Malacca, Britain to the north and the Dutch to the south. It is the origin of the border between Malaysia and Indonesia.
  • Penang, Malacca and Singapore became the Straits Settlements in 1826.

In the 1800s Chinese miners poured in to dig tin. From 1874 British advisers, called Residents, took charge of the inland states, and four of them were joined as the Federated Malay States in 1895. Rubber plantations from the 1890s brought workers from south India. In Borneo, James Brooke became Rajah of Sarawak in 1841. Malaya became independent in 1957 and joined Malaysia in 1963.
